overview: The Czech Republic, also called Czechia, became a separate country on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia. Its modern story includes international research, new infrastructure and the continued care of much older crafts. The map begins this label in 1994, one year after independence.

periods.title: The independent Czech Republic
periods.summary: A continuing republic emerged from the negotiated division of the Czechoslovak federation.

items.text: At ELI Beamlines near Prague, extremely intense laser pulses help scientists study matter under unusual conditions. The HAPLS laser grew from cooperation with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States and was integrated into the Czech facility in 2018.

A large research laser needs much more than a bright beam. ELI’s engineering includes pulse compression, measurement equipment and computerized control, while helium cooling helps manage heat in the amplifiers. Getting the experiment ready is a team effort involving optics, software and precise machinery.

Prague’s wastewater works were badly affected by the 2002 flood. The later New Water Line was designed with a watertight structure so floodwater could pass over it while protecting the equipment inside. The city planned for the river to rise again.

Parts of the rebuilt treatment-plant area became a public park with paths and river views. A roughly two-hundred-year-old oak influenced the site’s eastern boundary. Sewage treatment and a pleasant walk can share an address, provided the engineering is doing its job.

The government describes nine years of compulsory schooling. This common basic stage gives children a shared educational foundation before later choices of study. It belongs to the modern system; school arrangements changed considerably over the longer history of the Czech lands.

sections.title: Things made by hand, often together

items.text: Puppet theatre combines wood carving, costume making, writing and performance. Traveling puppeteer families helped establish traditions later adapted to local speech and comic characters. Today, practice and workshops keep those skills moving between generations in both Czechia and Slovakia.

Traditional blueprinted cloth starts with a protective paste stamped onto fabric. Indigo dye colors the exposed cloth while the covered areas keep their pattern. Family workshops preserve carved printing blocks and recipe notebooks. The technique is shared with several neighboring countries.

Glass-bead Christmas ornaments begin with a heated glass tube blown into a brass mold. Makers silver and color the resulting beads, then thread cut pieces onto wires. A delicate star can be assembled from many tiny glass parts rather than blown as one object.

In northern Bohemia, ornament making has passed through families and home workshops. UNESCO’s account identifies the Kulhavý workshop as the one that survived a difficult period of economic change, working with domestic bead makers. Museums and classes now help teach the craft.

Around Žatec, hop fields connect with drying buildings, warehouses and the town’s trading facilities. Tall supports and wires guide the climbing plants. This is an agricultural landscape whose work continues beyond harvest, through drying, sorting and storage.

Žatec’s industrial buildings preserve specialized equipment and spaces for drying, packing and certifying hops. Some continue their original work; others have new uses. The chimneys and warehouses record how a crop could shape a town’s streets and skyline.

Czech, article 1 of the constitution adopted in 1992: “Česká republika je svrchovaný, jednotný a demokratický právní stát”. Translation: “The Czech Republic is a sovereign, unified and democratic state governed by law.” This is an excerpt from the enacted text, which took effect on 1 January 1993.

ending.text: Czechia continues as an independent republic. Its creation in 1993 was a constitutional separation from Slovakia, with shared cultural and family ties continuing across the new border.
